newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.African growth slows, but manufacturing looks up.
newsitem.headline: S.African growth slows, but manufacturing looks up.

text.p: South Africa's economy grew by a modest 3.1 percent in 1996, despite a bumper agricultural season, the Central Statistical Service said on Thursday.

For the current year economists predict growth will slow to two to three percent as high interest rates bite and maize farmers fear a return of drought. But there should be a silver lining in an improving export-led manufacturing sector.
The final figure for real growth in gross domestic product (GDP) in 1996 was broadly in line with economists' expectations and compared with growth figure of 3.4 percent in 1995.
The farming sector, which enjoyed the best rains in years in 1996, saw output leap by 25.8 percent, making it the main contributor to growth.

The non-agricultural sector expanded output by just 1.9 percent in 1996 from 3.9 percent in 1995, mainly as a result of stagnation in manufacturing which expanded 0.4 percent from 7.6 percent in 1995.
This year the tables could be turned, with farmers expecting smaller crops -- especially if maize lands do not receive good rains in the next few weeks.

At the same time the hard-pressed manufacturing sector should be in for a revival, helped by a boom in exports following the rand's loss of a fifth of its value against a basket of currencies in 1996.

Signs of the potential turnaround are already evident in figures for the fourth quarter when manufacturing expanded 2.2 percent. That helped lift overall GDP growth in the period to 3.3 percent from 3.2 percent in the third quarter.
Dennis Dykes, chief economist at Nedcor bank, said manufacturing, along with mining and services, should continue to build output in 1997.
But the overall figure would be pulled back by agriculture.
"The fourth quarter on the face of it looks good, but obviously agricultural production boosted it quite significantly, so we are still looking at about two percent for 1997," Dykes said.

Reserve Bank Governor Chris Stals said earlier this month that South Africa's economy could expand by two to three percent in 1997 and he cautioned economists not to take an excessively pessimistic view of growth prospects.
Stals said South African manufacturing firms, enjoying a lower rand, were well-placed to take advantage of export opportunities in 1997 which in turn should boost the country's balance of payments.

The first trade data for the new year was also released on Thursday, showing a healthy rise in exports. They surged to 11.3 billion rand ($2.54 billion) in January from 10.5 billion in December and 7.4 billion a year ago.
With imports totalling 10.7 billion rand, South Africa recorded a trade surplus of 517.20 million in January against a deficit of close to one billion rand in January 1996.
